title: The Pre-Season Outlay: Why a Sporting Club or Academy Pays Months Before a Member Signs Up
excerpt: Coaching contracts, ground hire and equipment orders are already locked in for the summer season. The fees that pay for them are only just starting to land, and growth makes that gap wider, not smaller.
content:
Cricket academies, swim schools and netball associations are all moving through the same week right now. Coaches have been booked for the season, pool and ground hire is locked in through to autumn, and the first order of uniforms and equipment has already gone out the door. Enrolments are open and filling steadily. The fees that pay for all of it are not landing anywhere near as fast as the costs did.

That gap is not a sign anything has gone wrong. It is the ordinary shape of a season based business, and it turns up in some form every single year. The surprise is not that it happens. It is how often it still catches experienced operators who have run the same season a dozen times before, usually because the plan was built around the season's total revenue rather than the week by week timing of when that revenue actually clears, which is the heart of real cash flow discipline rather than a one-off budget exercise.

The cost curve runs ahead of the revenue curve

A club or academy commits to most of its season cost before the first session runs. Coaching fees, facility hire, insurance and affiliation renewals and the uniform or equipment order are either paid upfront or invoiced within the first few weeks of the term, because that is how most suppliers and venues price a season. Membership and term fees move at a different pace entirely. Some families pay the full term upfront. A larger share pay in instalments, pay late, or sign up partway through the term once word spreads that sessions are running well. None of that is a problem on its own. The problem is that the cost curve and the revenue curve are shaped completely differently, and almost nobody draws them on the same page before the season starts.

Growth makes the gap wider, not smaller

The instinct is that a bigger season should ease the squeeze, because more members means more fees coming in. In practice, growth usually makes the timing gap wider rather than narrower. More members means another coach, another hired court or lane, a bigger uniform order and a higher insurance premium, and all of that scales with the capacity being added, not with how quickly those new members actually pay. The fees from a bigger enrolment still arrive on the same instalment schedule as always. The costs of serving that bigger enrolment land in the same tight window they always have. A club that grows meaningfully from one season to the next can walk into November with a cash position that feels tighter than the smaller season before it, even though the eventual season profit is stronger.

What a season mapped in weeks actually shows

Most clubs and academies budget a season in one number, total revenue against total cost, reviewed after the fact or glanced at once a month. That tells a committee or an owner whether the season worked. It does not tell them whether the bank account will hold through the three or four weeks where coaching invoices, ground hire and insurance renewals land before enrolment fees have caught up. Mapping the season week by week, rather than as a single total, is what actually shows where that pinch point sits and how large a buffer needs to be to get through it without drawing on a facility at the worst possible moment. It is exactly the kind of forward view a 13-Week Cash Flow Build is designed to produce, built around the actual pattern of coaching costs, facility invoices and instalment income rather than an assumed even spread across the term.

None of this means a growing club or academy is being run poorly. It usually means the opposite, that enrolments are strong enough to justify the extra coaching and facility capacity committed to before the season begins. What separates the operators who feel in control of the season from the ones reacting to it is whether anyone mapped the weeks between the invoice and the instalment before the season started, rather than finding out in real time. For clubs and academies weighing up whether that kind of forward visibility is worth building in-house or bringing in, fractional CFO support during a season's build-up is usually a short, defined piece of work rather than an ongoing cost.

faqs.q: Why do sporting clubs and academies run short on cash right before the season starts?
faqs.a: Most of a season's cost, coaching fees, facility hire, insurance and equipment orders, is committed or invoiced in the weeks before the first session runs. Membership and term fees arrive on a slower, more staggered schedule, often across instalments through the term. The mismatch between when the money goes out and when it comes in is the usual cause, not a sign the season itself is underperforming.

faqs.q: Does a bigger enrolment season actually make the cash timing easier?
faqs.a: Not usually. A larger season needs more coaching capacity, more facility hire and a bigger equipment order, and all of that scales with the enrolments being added rather than with how quickly those new members pay. The costs still land in the same tight pre-season window, which is why growth tends to make the gap feel wider before it makes the season more profitable, the exact pattern a 13-Week Cash Flow Build is built to map out in advance.

faqs.q: How far ahead should a club or academy plan its season cash flow?
faqs.a: Mapping the season in weekly detail, from the point coaching contracts and facility bookings are confirmed through to when term fees are fully collected, gives a far clearer picture than a single season total. For most cricket, swimming and netball seasons that means starting the forecast several weeks before the first session, because that is typically when the bulk of the upfront costs are already committed.

faqs.q: Should membership fees be collected upfront instead of in instalments?
faqs.a: Instalments usually help enrolment and retention, so moving to full upfront payment is not always the right fix. The more useful question is whether the instalment schedule and the supplier payment terms have ever been compared side by side. Often the business can keep offering instalments and still close the gap, once it has visibility over exactly where the pinch points sit.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a profitable season and a cash positive one?
faqs.a: A season can be clearly profitable once every fee is collected and every cost is paid, and still put real pressure on the bank account while that is happening. Profit measures the whole season after the fact. Cash flow measures whether the money is actually there on the week an invoice or a wage run falls due, which is why a club can be growing and profitable while still feeling stretched in spring.

faqs.q: Is fractional CFO support worth it for a seasonal club or academy?
faqs.a: For many clubs and academies, the need is sharpest for a defined period around the season's build-up rather than all year round. Fractional CFO support brought in for that window can build the cash flow view, help set up a facility if one is needed, and hand over a repeatable process the club can run itself in future seasons, rather than becoming a permanent fixed cost.

faqs.q: What should a club do if it finds itself short on cash right before the season starts?
faqs.a: The first step is establishing exactly how temporary the gap is and when enrolment income is expected to close it, rather than reacting to the bank balance alone. From there, a short term facility arranged in advance on reasonable terms is usually a far better option than scrambling for one once the shortfall has already arrived.
